about: Every source of the types of reactions lab's record (docs/research/reactions/reactions.json) and of its primer (src/chem-data/reactions/primer.ts). Each was read for this lab on the retrieval date: eleven pages fetched that day, and six that an earlier lab also lists, read in the page that lab saved and not fetched again. No source has a copy in this folder. `fetchedSha256` is the sha256 of the file as it was fetched or read: a record of which file was read, not the hash of anything here, and nothing checks it. Each `supports` row names in `fields` the stored values it supports, each by its place in the record with the item's id in brackets (species[zinc], stations[peroxide].vessels[tube].after.gas); gives in `prints` a word, a formula, a label or a heading as the source prints it; and says in `where`, in this project's words, where that is, what the source says there, and how far the stored value goes beyond it. A row whose field is `primer` marks a source the primer rests on. The build holds the record to these rows: every source a value cites must have a row that names the value. No source is quoted beyond such words, formulas, labels and headings. Six sources are also listed by other labs' manifests and are written here as they are in src/chem-data/sources.json, so that the build lists each once: five pages on the reactions of one metal's ions, and one safety data sheet. The safety data sheets behind the bottles' hazards are in hazard-manifest.json; the record cites eight of them for what a bottle is and what its liquid looks like.

sources.citation: Santa Monica College. 6: Types of Chemical Reactions (Experiment). In Online Chemistry Lab Manual, Chem 11 Experiments; LibreTexts; read and not kept (retrieved 2026-10-12).

supports.where: The heading over the page's account of the kinds of reaction. The equations under it print H2O with (l), and CaCl2, NaCl and NaOH each with (aq). Sodium carbonate's formula is printed there too, once as a solid dropped into acid; that it is written (aq) here follows from the page's table of solubility, which gives the carbonates of the first group as soluble. The names are the usual ones for these formulas.

supports.prints: Displacement of hydrogen gas from an acid by a metal:
supports.where: Under Reaction Types, one of the page's four examples of a displacement reaction, which it also calls a single replacement: the equation that follows is magnesium with hydrochloric acid.

The start of the general form the page gives for an exchange reaction, which it also calls a double replacement: two compounds that make ions in solution change partners. It names the making of a solid that does not dissolve as one of three things that let such a reaction go.

supports.prints: Carbonates, Chromates and Phosphates are insoluble.
supports.where: The page's table of solubility. Its first row gives every compound of the first group of metals as soluble, and the row for chlorides gives them as soluble but for three metals, none of them sodium. So calcium carbonate is the solid and sodium chloride stays dissolved. The page does not print this equation: it is written from the general form and the table, and balanced by counting, which is this project's working.

supports.prints: Do not stare directly at the magnesium when it burns
supports.where: The safety lines before the instructions; the sentence goes on to say what the light can do to the eyes. The page's introduction lists the signs that go with a reaction: a change of colour, a solid forming, a gas bubbling off, heat given out or taken in, and one metal plating out on another. Under Reaction Types it says that magnesium is used in fireworks, that an exchange reaction softens hard water by taking its calcium out as a solid, and that a metal that pushes hydrogen out of an acid is more active than hydrogen. Its instructions ask for the state of each thing in an equation.

sources.citation: Soult, A. 11.3: Types of Inorganic Reactions. In Chemistry for Allied Health (University of Kentucky CHE 103); LibreTexts; read and not kept (retrieved 2026-10-12).

supports.prints: The general form of a combination reaction is:
supports.where: The sentence before the first of the four patterns in letters; each of the other three kinds has such a sentence and its pattern under its own heading. The page has a fifth kind, combustion, which this lab does not use. The patterns are stored as the page prints them; the page puts AC before B in the third and AD before CB in the fourth.

The heading. Under it the page says that such a reaction is also called a single displacement, which is the word another source uses of zinc in copper(II) sulfate solution, and gives zinc with hydrochloric acid as one, with its equation.

Under Combination Reactions: the page says that lit magnesium joins with the oxygen of the air and leaves this as a fine powder, and prints the equation with its states, two of magnesium to one of oxygen. The page does not give the powder's colour, which is another source's.
The heading of the first kind. The equations under it and under the next heading print O2, Cl2 and CO2 each as a gas, and MgO and CaCO3 each as a solid. The names are the page's.

supports.where: The heading. Under it the page says what a balanced equation is, what a coefficient is, that the small numbers inside a formula are never changed, and that no coefficient is written for one; it works an example by counting the atoms on each side.

supports.prints: A displacement reaction between iron and copper(II) sulfate solution
supports.where: The heading. The equation under it prints Cu with (s) and CuSO4 with (aq).

supports.prints: Displacement reactions and the reactivity series
supports.where: The heading. Under it the page says that a metal higher in the series pushes one lower down out of its salts. Before it the page writes the equation for iron in copper(II) sulfate solution and says that the missing blue shows the copper(II) sulfate has gone. The page does not write the equation for zinc: it is the iron equation with zinc and zinc sulfate, whose formula another page prints, which is this project's working.

sources.citation: Clark, J. Chemguide: Reactions between Metals and Dilute Acids; read and not kept (retrieved 2026-10-12).

supports.prints: Taking a closer look at two of the metals commonly reacted with acids
supports.where: The heading. The equations under it print Mg and Zn each with (s); HCl, MgCl2, ZnCl2 and ZnSO4 each with (aq); and H2 with (g). The names of the two chlorides and of zinc sulfate are the usual ones for these formulas.

The start of the summary the page gives in words, which ends in a salt and hydrogen. Under the heading for each metal it writes the equation with dilute hydrochloric acid, one of the metal to two of the acid, and calls the gas hydrogen.

supports.prints: What you should be comfortable with before you go on
supports.where: The heading. Under it the page says that the metals above hydrogen in the series react with acids and those below it do not, and that the reactions get faster the further up the series a metal stands; further down it calls zinc a little slow with dilute acids in the cold. That magnesium is stored as fast and zinc as slow is this reading of those two sentences with the two metals' places in the series; the page gives no rate for either. Copper is not named on the page: its place below hydrogen is another page's.

supports.prints: Most metals react to give hydrogen and a colourless solution
supports.where: A note near the head of the page. The page writes zinc with dilute sulfuric acid giving ZnSO4(aq), which is where the formula of zinc sulfate in this equation is from, and by the note that solution has no colour.

supports.prints: A catalyst is chemically unchanged at the end of a reaction
supports.where: Under the heading on making hydrogen from zinc in the laboratory, where the page says why a thing added there is not a catalyst.

sources.citation: Clark, J. Chemguide: An Introduction to the Reactivity Series; read and not kept (retrieved 2026-10-12).

supports.where: The label at the head of the page's list, which runs down to the least reactive. Magnesium stands fifth in it; zinc is two metals lower, with carbon between; hydrogen, in brackets, is three places below zinc; and copper is the next after hydrogen. So the three metals of this lab run magnesium, zinc, copper, with hydrogen between the last two. The order is stored from this list, and not worked out from standard potentials.

supports.where: Under the heading on the reactions with oxygen, of magnesium. The record stores a white light.

The heading. Under it the page says that the metals of this group all take up nitrogen as well when they burn in air, and that the white ash of magnesium ribbon burnt in air is the oxide and the nitride mixed. It gives no proportion, and the note gives none.

sources.citation: Royal Society of Chemistry. Observing chemical changes: a microscale class experiment. RSC Education; read and not kept (retrieved 2026-10-12).

supports.where: The heading. The tenth note under it is for a piece of zinc in copper(II) sulfate solution: the zinc's surface turns red-brown as copper comes out on it, by what the page calls a displacement, and the solution's blue fades. The page's solution is 0.2 M and a few drops; that a tube of the 1 M solution fades to a paler blue and not to no colour is this lab's reading of the word fades.

sources.citation: Modic, A. L. Thought lab: Catalysts and hydrogen peroxide. Chem 13 News Magazine, November 2017; University of Waterloo; read and not kept (retrieved 2026-10-12).

supports.where: The heading. The paragraph under it says that hydrogen peroxide in water comes apart slowly by itself into oxygen gas and water, names iron(III) chloride as one of three things that speed this up as catalysts, and says that light does it too, which is why the bottles are dark. The page has 6% peroxide and solid iron(III) chloride; that bubbles are seen in a tube of 3% with a few drops of the solution is this lab's reading. It gives no colour for the liquid.

In the last of the page's questions: the enthalpy of the reaction for each mole of hydrogen peroxide, a negative figure, so heat is given out. That the tube is felt to warm is this lab's reading; the page gives no rise in temperature.

sources.citation: Lower, S. 17.6: Catalysts and Catalysis. In Chem1 Virtual Textbook, Chemical Kinetics and Dynamics; LibreTexts; read and not kept (retrieved 2026-10-12).

supports.where: The heading. Under it the page prints the equation, two of the peroxide giving two of water and one of oxygen, with no states, and says that this is very slow with nothing added, that many things speed it up greatly, and that heat comes off as they do. The states are this lab's: the peroxide is a 3% solution in water, written (aq), and (l) is taken too, since the pure substance is a liquid.

The heading. Under it the page says that a catalyst speeds a reaction up, is not used up by it and has no place in the equation for the whole change. Further down, under a heading that comes back to hydrogen peroxide, it shows iron ions spent in one step and made again in the next.
